```{r, include = FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

This vignette shows how to match species names before classifying vegetation
plots with `resy_classify()`. Each expert system uses a particular set of species
names, and the names in your plot data need to match.

The EUNIS expert system (Chytrý et al.
[2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519)), for example, uses the same species
names as the European Vegetation Archive (Chytrý et al. [2016](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12191)),
so data from there can be used
directly. Data following other taxonomic sources, such as [GBIF](https://www.gbif.org/),
[World Flora Online](https://www.worldfloraonline.org/), [POWO](https://powo.science.kew.org/)
or a national checklist, may use synonyms, different author citations or
spelling variants. RESY matches these names in a separate step so
you can review the matches before classification.

1. **Resolve** the species names with `resy_resolve_taxa()`.
2. **Inspect** the matches with [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html).
3. **Classify** the vegetation surveys with the resolved data with `resy_classify()`.

## Example

The following R packages are required to run the example of this vignette:

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(RESY)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
```

```{r build-info, include=FALSE}
build <- utils::read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "esy_synonyms_build.csv", package = "RESY"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
backbones <- utils::read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "esy_synonyms_backbones.csv", package = "RESY"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = ""
)
bb <- function(name, col) backbones[[col]][backbones$backbone == name]
pct <- function(x, n) round(100 * x / n)
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

### Resolve names

`resy_resolve_taxa()` maps a column of names to the species names of an expert
system, called the canonical names. By default, these are the species names of
the EUNIS expert system, which ship with RESY. They come from the expert system
itself, not from a taxonomic database, but
`r pct(build$n_esy_canonical_euromed, build$n_esy_canonical)`% of them
(`r big(build$n_esy_canonical_euromed)` of `r big(build$n_esy_canonical)`) are
accepted names in Euro+Med PlantBase (release `r bb("euromed", "version")`).

Each name is looked up in up to four steps, and the first step that finds it
sets the match type:

1. The name is a canonical name (`"exact"`).
2. The name is in the synonym table (`"synonym"`), described in
   [The shipped synonym table](#the-shipped-synonym-table).
3. With its author citation removed by `resy_clean_names()`, the name is a
   canonical name (`"cleaned_exact"`).
4. With its author citation removed, the name is in the synonym table
   (`"cleaned_synonym"`).

The name without author citation is used only for the lookup; the name column
in your data keeps the name as submitted. A name that none of the four steps
finds stays `NA` and is flagged `"unresolved"`. Nothing is ever replaced with a
best guess.

```{r resolve}
plots <- data.frame(
  TaxonName = c(
    "Hibiscus praecox",        # a synonym in the shipped table
    "Abelmoschus longifolius",  # another synonym
    "Fagus sylvatica",          # already a canonical name
    "Anemone nemorosa L.",      # canonical name with an author citation
    "Not a real species 123"    # resolves to nothing
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

resolved <- resy_resolve_taxa(plots, species_col = "TaxonName")
resolved
```

The result is a `resy_taxa` table, the same kind `resy_check_taxonomy()`
returns. `summary()` reports how many names and records resolved, the records by
match type, and the distinct names that stayed unresolved.

```{r summarise}
summary(resolved)
```

Unresolved names can be fixed by correcting a spelling, adding a row to your own
crosswalk (see [Bring your own crosswalk](#bring-your-own-crosswalk)), or
leaving them out.

### The shipped synonym table

RESY ships a synonym table built for the EUNIS expert system: it maps alternate
species names to the names that EUNIS uses. It pools the synonyms of six taxonomic backbones, the reference lists of
accepted names and their synonyms that taxonomic databases publish
(Euro+Med (europlusmed.org), [WFO](https://www.worldfloraonline.org/),
[GBIF](https://www.gbif.org/),
[Catalogue of Life](https://www.catalogueoflife.org/),
[ITIS](https://www.itis.gov/),
[NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/taxonomy/)),
so a name coming from any
of them can resolve without you having to say which backbone it came from. With
another expert system, the table resolves only names that point to a species
name the two systems share; for the other names, use your own synonym table
(see [Bring your own crosswalk](#bring-your-own-crosswalk)).

The table was built on `r build$built` against the `r build$expert_system`
expert system `r build$expert_version`, from the backbone releases below.
`data-raw/build_synonyms.R` in the source repository rebuilds it with taxify
`r build$taxify_version` (Colling [2026](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.taxify)).

```{r build-backbones, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Backbone      = backbones$backbone,
    `Upstream data` = ifelse(is.na(backbones$upstream_date), "", backbones$upstream_date),
    check.names   = FALSE
  )
)
```

The synonyms are binomials (genus and species epithet). Infraspecific names,
hybrid formulas, and bare genera are not in the table, so a name of that kind is
not resolved through it.

`resy_read_synonyms()` without arguments reads the shipped table:

```{r shipped-table}
syn <- resy_read_synonyms()
nrow(syn)
head(syn)
```

Each row of the shipped table is a synonym pair: an alternate spelling
(`synonym`) and the EUNIS name it resolves to (`esy_canonical`), with the
backbone(s) that list the synonym under that name (`source`). The column
`accepted_in` names the backbones that list the same synonym as an accepted
name of its own, by the same author as in the backbones of `source` (an accepted
name by another author is a different taxon with the same name and is not
counted). A backbone appears in both `source` and `accepted_in` when it holds
an accepted row and a synonym row for the name.

The column is empty for
`r round(100 * mean(is.na(syn$accepted_in)))`% of the synonym pairs: no backbone
accepts these synonyms as species of their own, so every backbone that lists the
name agrees that it is a synonym. A filled `accepted_in` marks a name that one
backbone treats as a synonym and another as a separate species:

```{r accepted-in}
head(syn[!is.na(syn$accepted_in), ], 4)
```

A synonym pair with several backbones in `source` is counted once for each of them, so
the counts per backbone add up to more than the number of rows.

```{r support-table}
per_backbone <- table(unlist(strsplit(syn$source, ";", fixed = TRUE)))
support <- data.frame(
  backbone = names(per_backbone),
  pairs    = as.integer(per_backbone),
  share    = round(100 * as.integer(per_backbone) / nrow(syn), 1)
)
support <- support[order(-support$pairs), ]

knitr::kable(
  support,
  row.names   = FALSE,
  col.names   = c("Backbone", "Synonym pairs", "% of table"),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
)
```

GBIF supports the most synonym pairs and Euro+Med the fewest, for two reasons
measured on the backbone releases above. The GBIF backbone holds
`r big(bb("gbif", "synonym_rows"))` synonym rows, the Euro+Med backbone
`r big(bb("euromed", "synonym_rows"))`. And most Euro+Med synonymy is already
part of the expert system: of the Euro+Med synonyms that point to a EUNIS name,
`r pct(bb("euromed", "synonyms_in_expert"), bb("euromed", "synonyms_to_esy"))`%
are names the expert system lists in its own species aggregation, so the
classifier already counts them and the table leaves them out. For GBIF, this
share is
`r pct(bb("gbif", "synonyms_in_expert"), bb("gbif", "synonyms_to_esy"))`%.

Most synonym pairs are supported by more than one backbone:

```{r support-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3}
per_pair <- table(lengths(strsplit(syn$source, ";", fixed = TRUE)))
support_n <- data.frame(
  n_backbones = names(per_pair),
  pairs       = as.integer(per_pair)
)

ggplot(support_n, aes(x = n_backbones, y = pairs)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = "Number of backbones supporting a synonym pair", y = "Synonym pairs") +
  theme_classic()
```

### Bring your own crosswalk

A crosswalk is a table that maps each name of one name list to the matching
name in another, here from the names in your data to the canonical names of the
expert system. The shipped synonym table is one; `resy_resolve_taxa()` also
accepts your own, with three columns: `synonym`, `esy_canonical`, and `source`.
It can come from a national checklist, a Turboveg species list, or a
name-matching package such as [taxify](https://github.com/gcol33/taxify) or
[taxize](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.taxize) (Chamberlain & Szocs
[2013](https://f1000research.com/articles/2-191/v2)). A small example ships with the package.

```{r own-csv}
cw_path <- system.file("extdata", "example_crosswalk.csv", package = "RESY")
crosswalk <- resy_read_synonyms(cw_path)
crosswalk
```

Pass it to `synonyms=`, and give the target names to `canonical=` so resolution
uses your table alone:

```{r own-resolve}
my_plots <- data.frame(
  TaxonName = c("Fagus silvatica", "Abies pectinata", "Quercus robur"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

resy_resolve_taxa(
  my_plots,
  species_col = "TaxonName",
  synonyms    = crosswalk,
  canonical   = unique(crosswalk$esy_canonical)
)
```

If your crosswalk lives in an Excel sheet, read it yourself and pass the data
frame. RESY validates the columns and uses it directly, so it needs no Excel
package as a dependency:

```{r excel, eval=FALSE}
crosswalk <- readxl::read_excel("my_crosswalk.xlsx")
resy_resolve_taxa(my_plots, synonyms = crosswalk,
                  canonical = unique(crosswalk$esy_canonical))
```

A synonym that maps to more than one canonical name is dropped, so an ambiguous
table cannot produce a silent substitution.

### Classify the resolved data

Once the names match the species list of the expert system, classify as in
[Get started](RESY.html).
Resolve them against the species list of the expert system you classify with
(here `Apennine-test`), write the resolved name back to the name column, keeping the original
where a name did not resolve, and pass the result to `resy_classify()`. The species list is taken from
`expert$aggs`, which holds the taxa of the expert system: each name is a taxon
the rules use, and its elements are the names counted as that taxon.

```{r classify, message=FALSE}
species <- read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_species.csv", package = "RESY"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
species <- head(species, 200)   # keep the example quick

obs <- data.frame(
  PlotObservationID = species$PlotObservationID,
  TaxonName         = species$scientificName,
  Cover_Perc        = species$Cover_Perc,
  stringsAsFactors  = FALSE
)
expert <- resy_load_expert(scheme = "Apennine-test")
expert_vocab <- unique(c(names(expert$aggs), unlist(expert$aggs, use.names = FALSE)))

resolved_obs <- resy_resolve_taxa(
  obs, species_col = "TaxonName", canonical = expert_vocab
)
table(resolved_obs$taxon_confidence)

resolved_obs$TaxonName <- ifelse(
  is.na(resolved_obs$canonical), resolved_obs$TaxonName, resolved_obs$canonical
)
obs <- resolved_obs[c("PlotObservationID", "TaxonName", "Cover_Perc")]
header <- as.data.frame(unique(obs["PlotObservationID"]))

res <- resy_classify(obs, header, scheme = "Apennine-test")
head(res$result.classification)
```

For a quick pass, `resy_classify(..., resolve_taxa = TRUE)` runs the resolution
against the species list of the expert system and then classifies in a single call, and reports
what it did in `res$taxon_resolution`. The two-step route above is recommended,
since it lets you check the unresolved names before they reach the classifier.
